# Onity AI Usage Guide

This guide is written for coding assistants and dense enough for people: the rules that produce
correct Onity code, the canonical scene, a per-module API index and an error-to-fix table. Onity
(`com.onity.framework`, Unity 2022.3 LTS or newer) puts dependency injection, reactive state, typed
messaging, factories with pooling and `OnityTask` async in one package with one lifetime model: a scope
owns its services, subscriptions, tasks and pools and disposes them together. Every name here was
checked against the 0.6 source; the installed package source (`Runtime/`) and tests (`Tests/`) win when
a sentence and the code disagree.

- The core assemblies (`Onity.Core`, `Onity.DI`, `Onity.Reactive`, `Onity.Messaging`, `Onity.Factory`,
  `Onity.Composition`) are engine-free (no `UnityEngine`). The Unity glue lives in `Onity.Unity`
  (`Onity.Unity.Contexts`, `Onity.Unity.Installers`, `Onity.Unity.Messaging`, `Onity.Unity.Reactive`,
  `Onity.Unity.Async`, `Onity.Unity.Input`) and the optional `Onity.Unity.UGUI`.
- Hot paths avoid per-call managed allocation: resolve, `Publish`, `OnNext`, the frame streams and the
  pooled task sources allocate only the objects a call must create (a transient resolve still allocates
  the instance it returns). The runtime uses no `System.Linq` and has no non-Unity third-party
  dependency. Measured results, with their conditions, are on the
  [Comparisons](https://furkantokkan.github.io/Onity/comparisons/) pages; this guide states no numbers.
- Package code style: Allman braces, private instance fields `m_camelCase`, private static
  `s_camelCase`, constants `k_camelCase`. Match it when adding code to the package; your own game code
  can follow its own conventions.

Sections: 1 overview, 2 DI, 3 reactive, 4 events, 5 the canonical scene, 6 DO and DON'T, 7 API index,
8 errors, 9 the events decision rule, 10 factories and pooling, 11 async.

---

## 1. One package, one lifetime model

You do not stitch a container, a reactive library, a message bus and an async library together. Onity
is one API with one mental model:

```text
DI is the spine.             Bind services in a MonoInstaller; the container constructs them with their dependencies.
Events ride the broker.      Every context binds MessageBroker and OnityEventHub; OnityEvent is the Unity shorthand.
Reactive rides both.         Subject<T>, ReactiveProperty<T> and Observe<T>() are the same IOnityObservable<T>.
Async ends with its owner.   OnityTask work takes the scope token or the destroy token; it stops before the services it uses are disposed.
Pools belong to the scope.   BindPooledFactory binds IFactory<T> to spawn and IPool<T> to release; the scope disposes the pool.
Lifetime is one rule.        Every Subscribe returns IDisposable; retain it with AddTo(this), TakeUntilDisable(this), AddTo(scope) or AddTo(bag).
```

The whole framework in ten lines:

```csharp
// 1. Register in an installer:           container.Bind<IScoreService>().To<ScoreService>().AsSingle();
// 2. Consume by constructor injection:    public HealthService(ReactiveProperty<int> health, ISubscriber<PlayerDamaged> damage, IOnityScopeLifetime scope) { ... }
// 3. Inject a MonoBehaviour's members:    [Inject] private IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<int> m_health;
// 4. Hold current state:                  container.BindReactiveProperty(initialValue: 100);   // ReactiveProperty<int> + IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<int>
// 5. Observe state (current value first): m_health.Subscribe(value => Show(value)).TakeUntilDisable(this);
// 6. Publish a message:                   OnityEvent.Publish(this, new PlayerDamaged(25));
// 7. Receive it as a filtered stream:     OnityEvent.Observe<PlayerDamaged>(this).Where(m => m.Amount >= 10).Subscribe(ShowHit).TakeUntilDisable(this);
// 8. Tie a service subscription to its scope: damage.Subscribe(OnDamaged).AddTo(scope);
// 9. Run an async loop that ends with the scope: RegenerateAsync(m_scope.Token).Forget();   // async OnityTaskVoid
// 10. Spawn and release from a pool:       HitMarker marker = m_hitMarkers.Create(); ... m_hitMarkerPool.Release(marker);
```

Why one package instead of four libraries:

| Concern | Separate libraries | Onity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mental models | a container, an observable type, a bus with filters, an async type, each with its own idiom | one `OnityContainer` spine, one `IOnityObservable<T>`, one `OnityTask` |
| Event to stream | hand-written adapter from the bus to the reactive library | `Observe<T>()` returns `IOnityObservable<T>` |
| Disposal | one idiom per library | `IDisposable` plus `AddTo(...)` everywhere |
| DI and events wiring | a setup call plus per-type registrations | the broker and the hub are bound by every context |
| Async ownership | tokens you build and cancel yourself | the scope token (`IOnityScopeLifetime`) and destroy tokens, canceled before disposal |
| Engine coupling | varies | an engine-free, scene-free core |

---

## 2. DI: OnityContainer

`OnityContainer` (`Onity.DI`) is sealed, engine-free and parent-scoped, and implements `IResolver`,
`IOnityScopeLifetime` and `IDisposable`. It runs in an EditMode test with no scene:
`using OnityContainer container = new OnityContainer();`.

### 2.1 Binding surface

```csharp
using Onity.DI;                 // OnityContainer

using OnityContainer container = new OnityContainer();

// Contract -> implementation -> lifetime. The lifetime call registers the binding; Bind and To alone register nothing.
container.Bind<IScoreService>().To<ScoreService>().AsSingle();        // one instance in this scope, shared with children
container.Bind<IPathfinder>().To<AStarPathfinder>().AsTransient();   // a new instance per resolve
container.Bind<IMatchState>().To<MatchState>().AsScoped();           // one instance per resolving scope
container.Bind<IClock>().To<GameClock>().AsSingle().NonLazy();       // created during Build() instead of on first use

// Self-bind shorthand (To defaults to the contract type):
container.Bind<ScoreService>().AsSingle();

// Share ONE instance across the concrete type and all its interfaces (see the trap in 2.7):
container.BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<HealthService>().AsSingle();       // HealthService, IOnityInitializable, ...
container.BindInterfacesTo<HealthService>().AsSingle();              // interfaces only; throws when the type has none

// Identified and conditional bindings (configure before the lifetime):
container.Bind<IClock>().To<ReplayClock>().WithId("replay").AsSingle();
container.Bind<IClock>().To<EditorClock>().WhenInjectedInto<PreviewController>().AsSingle();

// A pre-built instance (caller-owned; null throws OnityBindingException):
container.BindInstance<IGameConfig>(loadedConfig);

// Factories (always bound AsSingle; you author the IFactory<...> class, see 2.5). Each form constrains TFactory
// to the contract it binds: BindFactory<TValue, TFactory>() needs an IFactory<TValue>, the one-parameter form an
// IFactory<TParam, TValue>, the two-parameter form an IFactory<TParam1, TParam2, TValue>:
container.BindFactory<EnemySpawnRequest, Enemy, EnemyFactory>();     // EnemyFactory : IFactory<EnemySpawnRequest, Enemy>
```

| Call | Namespace | Returns | Then |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Bind<TContract>()` | `Onity.DI` | `TypeBindingBuilder<TContract>` | optional `To<TConcrete>()`, `WithId(id)`, `WhenInjectedInto<TConsumer>()`; then `AsSingle()`, `AsScoped()`, `AsTransient()` or `FromSubContainerResolve(install)`; optional `NonLazy()` |
| `Bind(Type contractType)` | `Onity.DI` | `RuntimeTypeBindingBuilder` | the same with `To(Type)`; accepts open generic definitions |
| `BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<TConcrete>()` | `Onity.DI` | `MultiTypeBindingBuilder` | optional `WithId`, `WhenInjectedInto`; then `AsSingle()`, `AsScoped()` or `AsTransient()`; optional `NonLazy()` |
| `BindInterfacesTo<TConcrete>()` | `Onity.DI` | `MultiTypeBindingBuilder` | the same; the concrete type itself is not bound |
| `BindInstance<TContract>(instance)`, `BindInstance<TContract>(instance, id)` | `Onity.DI` | `void` | registers at once; the instance stays caller-owned |
| `BindFactory<TValue, TFactory>()` and the one- and two-parameter forms | `Onity.DI` | `void` | binds the factory with `BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<TFactory>().AsSingle()` |
| `Rebind<TContract>(id = null)`, `Rebind(Type, id = null)` | `Onity.DI` | a builder | replaces the local binding when the new lifetime is selected; works after `Build()` |
| `Unbind<TContract>(id = null)`, `Unbind(Type, id = null)` | `Onity.DI` | `bool` | removes the local binding; works after `Build()` |
| `BindReactiveProperty`, `BindSubject`, `DeclareMessage`, `DeclareAsyncMessage` | `Onity.Composition` | the primitive | one scope-owned primitive under its contracts (2.8, section 4) |
| `BindMessageChannel<T>()` | `Onity.Unity.Messaging` | `void` | `IPublisher<T>` and `ISubscriber<T>` on the scope broker's channel (section 4) |
| `BindPooledFactory(prefab, parent, defaultCapacity, maxSize)`, `BindPooledFactory(IPool<T>)` | `Onity.Unity.Installers` | `void` | `IPool<T>` and `IFactory<T>` (2.5, section 10) |
| `BindScriptableObject(asset)`, `BindScriptableObject<TContract, TAsset>(asset)` | `Onity.Unity.Installers` | `void` | member-injects the asset, then binds it as an instance |

`NonLazy()` throws `OnityBindingException` when it is called before the lifetime, on a conditional
binding, or on an open generic binding (the closed type is unknown until resolve).

### 2.2 Resolve and inject

```csharp
IScoreService score = container.Resolve<IScoreService>();                 // throws OnityResolveException when unresolvable
object service = container.Resolve(typeof(IScoreService));               // runtime-type form
IClock replay = container.Resolve<IClock>("replay");                      // identified form

if (container.TryResolve<IPathfinder>(out IPathfinder pathfinder)) { }    // false instead of throwing
if (container.TryResolve(typeof(IPathfinder), out object found)) { }
if (container.TryResolve<IClock>("replay", out IClock clock)) { }

bool resolvable = container.CanResolve(typeof(IScoreService));           // no construction
container.Inject(existingObject);                                         // member-inject an object you created
```

`OnityContainer` and `IResolver` always resolve to the active scope; a factory injects `IResolver` for
manual resolves. Resolve once and keep the reference: `Resolve` inside `Update` is a lookup per frame
for a value injection already handed you (`ONITY001`).

### 2.3 [Inject] on constructor, field, property, method and parameter

```csharp
using Onity.DI;                 // Inject

public sealed class CombatService
{
    private readonly IDamageCalculator m_damage;

    // Constructor injection is preferred. A single [Inject] constructor wins; otherwise the public
    // constructor with the most parameters. A non-public constructor is used only when no public one exists.
    public CombatService(IDamageCalculator damage)
    {
        m_damage = damage;
    }

    [Inject] private IClock m_clock;                       // field injection; private is fine
    [Inject] public IScoreService Score { get; set; }      // property injection; a setter is required
    [Inject] private IClock m_replayClock;                 // add Id = "replay" to select an identified binding

    [Inject]                                                // method injection; runs after fields and properties
    private void Configure(IGameConfig config)              // cannot be generic
    {
    }
}
```

Member injection runs base class first, then derived class, and within a type fields, then properties,
then methods. Static members are never injected. `[Inject(Id = ...)]` goes on a field, a property, or an
individual constructor or method parameter. These throw `OnityBindingException`: more than one `[Inject]`
constructor, an `[Inject]` property without a setter, an `[Inject]` indexer, and a generic `[Inject]`
method. A `MonoBehaviour` is injected by its context during the context's `Awake`, or later by
`context.InjectGameObject(root)` and `container.Inject(target)`; read injected members in `Start` or
later, not in field initializers.

### 2.4 Child containers, scoped lifetimes, identified and conditional bindings

```csharp
using OnityContainer parent = new OnityContainer();
parent.Bind<IClock>().To<GameClock>().AsSingle();
parent.Bind<IMatchState>().To<MatchState>().AsScoped();
parent.Build();

using OnityContainer child = new OnityContainer(parent);
child.Bind<IClock>().To<ReplayClock>().AsSingle();     // shadows IClock in the child only
child.Build();

// child.Resolve<IClock>()       -> ReplayClock
// parent.Resolve<IClock>()      -> GameClock
// child.Resolve<IMatchState>()  -> one child-owned MatchState on repeated calls
// parent.Resolve<IMatchState>() -> a separate parent-owned MatchState
```

- A child inherits the parent's bindings; a child binding shadows the parent's only inside the child.
  Disposing the child does not dispose the parent; disposing the parent cancels the child's scope token.
- `AsScoped()` is one instance per resolving scope, built with that scope's dependencies and disposed
  with it. VContainer's `Lifetime.Scoped` maps to it (the `Lifetime` enum in `Onity.Core` stays
  `{ Singleton, Transient }`; `AsScoped()` is a builder lifetime).
- `WithId(object id)` registers a second binding of the same contract under a value-compared id; consume
  it with `[Inject(Id = ...)]`, `Resolve<T>(id)` or `TryResolve<T>(id, out T)`. A missing id does not
  construct a service implicitly.
- `WhenInjectedInto<TConsumer>()` restricts a binding to one consumer type and its derived types. A
  matching conditional binding wins over the unconditional one in the same scope; two matching
  conditional bindings throw `OnityResolveException`; an unconditional binding in a child scope shadows
  conditional bindings in an ancestor.
- `FromSubContainerResolve(install)` replaces `To<C>()`: the installer runs once per requesting scope in
  a child container, must bind the exported contract there, and the requesting scope forwards ticks to
  that child and disposes it.
- `Unbind` and `Rebind` change the local scope only, also after `Build()`. A removed singleton stops
  ticking but stays owned; a rebound tickable stops the old instance and starts the replacement.

### 2.5 Factories (runtime arguments)

There is no `container.Instantiate<T>(args)` and no fluent factory body. To pass a runtime value into a
constructed object, author an `IFactory<...>` (`Onity.Factory`) and bind it with `BindFactory`; the
container constructs the factory and injects its collaborators, so only runtime values travel through
`Create`:

```csharp
using Onity.Factory;            // IFactory<TParam, TValue>

public sealed class EnemyFactory : IFactory<EnemySpawnRequest, Enemy>
{
    private readonly IClock m_clock;                       // injected into the factory

    public EnemyFactory(IClock clock)
    {
        m_clock = clock;
    }

    public Enemy Create(EnemySpawnRequest request)
    {
        return new Enemy(request.Id, request.Level, m_clock);
    }
}

// Registration and use (fragment):
// container.BindFactory<EnemySpawnRequest, Enemy, EnemyFactory>();
// Enemy elite = container.Resolve<IFactory<EnemySpawnRequest, Enemy>>().Create(new EnemySpawnRequest("elite", 5));
```

`BindFactory` facts: `where TFactory : class, IFactory<...>`; it registers
`BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<TFactory>().AsSingle()`, so the factory resolves as `IFactory<...>` and as its
own type, one instance per scope, created on first resolve; it returns `void`, so there is no
`AsTransient()` or `NonLazy()` form. Two parameters is the largest arity; wrap more values in a struct.
A container-built class cannot receive a per-call value (an id, a level, a position) through its
constructor: the container only supplies bound types, and resolving it throws `OnityResolveException`
(8.4). Inject the factory instead and call `Create(value)`.

Which factory or pool API:

| You need | Use | Registers | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A new plain object per call from 0, 1 or 2 runtime arguments | your `IFactory<...>` class and `BindFactory<...>()` | `IFactory<...>` and the factory type (one shared instance) | no pooling; you write `Create` |
| Reusable prefab instances, no arguments | `BindPooledFactory(prefab, parent, defaultCapacity, maxSize)` in a `MonoInstaller` | `IPool<TComponent>` (instance) and `IFactory<TComponent>` (`PooledFactory<TComponent>` singleton) | defaults 16 and 512; no prewarm, fixed-size or name option; the scope disposes the pool it creates (10.4) |
| A prefab pool with prewarm, fixed capacity, a create hook or a diagnostics name | `new PrefabComponentPool<T>(...)`, then `BindPooledFactory(pool)` | the same two bindings | caller-owned: `pool.AddTo(container)` or dispose it yourself (10.4) |
| A pool you already built, any item type | `BindPooledFactory(IPool<T>)` | the same two bindings | caller-owned; the container disposes it only after `pool.AddTo(container)` |
| Pooled spawn with 1 or 2 runtime arguments | `new PooledFactory<TParam, T>(pool, initialize)` or the two-parameter form, bound with `BindInstance<IFactory<TParam, T>>(...)` | what you bind | needs an `IParameterizedPool<T>`; `initialize` runs before the get hooks and activation (10.2) |
| Reusable plain C# objects, no `GameObject` | `new OnityObjectPool<T>(...)` (`T : class`), optionally `BindPooledFactory(pool)` | what you bind | reset in `actionOnGet` and `actionOnRelease`; `IPoolHooks` is not called (10.3) |

`BindPooledFactory` lives in `Onity.Unity.Installers`; `Onity.Pooling` references `UnityEngine` for
`PrefabComponentPool<T>`; the engine-free `Onity.DI` and `Onity.Factory` do not. Recipes, call order,
documented behaviors and lifetime rules: section 10.

### 2.6 Build and async startup

```csharp
container.RegisterBuildCallback(resolver => resolver.Resolve<IGameLoopRunner>().Start());               // runs in Build()
container.RegisterBuildCallbackAsync(async (resolver, token) => await resolver.Resolve<ISaveLoader>().PrimeAsync(token));

container.Build();                                // sync callbacks, Initialize(); idempotent
await container.BuildAsync(cancellationToken);   // Build(), async callbacks, then InitializeAsync() one at a time; result cached
```

Build callbacks cannot be registered after the build is finalized (`OnityBindingException`). Each async
step starts on the context the build started on, the main thread in a Unity context. The token the
callbacks and initializers receive is the scope's `LifetimeToken`, linked with the caller's token when
one is passed; disposing the container mid-run ends `BuildAsync` as canceled, and a canceled or faulted
run is not cached, so the next call resumes at the first incomplete step. `Dispose()` cancels
`LifetimeToken` first, then disposes installed child scopes, scoped instances and owned singletons in
reverse registration order. Scope tokens and async startup in a scene: 11.4.

### 2.7 Documented behaviors (test-locked): DO and DON'T

| Behavior | DO / DON'T |
| --- | --- |
| Implicit transients | An unbound concrete class resolves as a new instance per resolve. DON'T rely on it for shared state; bind it `AsSingle()`. |
| Unbound abstractions | An unbound interface, abstract class or open generic definition throws `OnityResolveException`. DO bind them. |
| Last binding wins | Binding the same contract twice replaces the first binding; there is no duplicate-binding error. DO use it to override; DON'T expect a conflict. |
| Distinct singletons | `Bind<IFoo>().To<C>()` plus `Bind<IBar>().To<C>()` create two `C` instances. DO use `BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<C>().AsSingle()` to share one. |
| Constructor selection | A single `[Inject]` constructor wins; otherwise the public constructor with the most parameters; a non-public constructor only when no public one exists. DON'T add a second `[Inject]` constructor. |
| Circular dependency | Constructor and member cycles throw `OnityResolveException` at resolve time with the full chain. DO break the cycle with a factory or `IResolver`. |
| Open generics | DO bind `Bind(typeof(IRepository<>)).To(typeof(Repository<>)).AsSingle()` and resolve closed forms such as `IRepository<PlayerProfile>`; on IL2CPP preserve the closed types. `NonLazy()` is not supported on an open generic binding. |
| Collection injection | DO request `IEnumerable<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>`, `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`, `IList<T>`, `ICollection<T>`, `List<T>` or `T[]` to receive every explicit binding of `T` from this scope and its ancestors, ancestors first. A plain `Resolve<T>()` returns the last binding. |
| Conditional and identified bindings | DO configure `WithId` and `WhenInjectedInto` before the lifetime. Two matching conditional bindings throw; a local unconditional binding shadows ancestor conditions; a missing id does not construct anything. |
| Post-build changes | `Unbind` and `Rebind` work after `Build()`; new bindings belong in installers before it, and build callbacks throw afterwards. |
| Statics | `[Inject]` on a static member is ignored. DON'T use it. |

### 2.8 Copy-paste installer recipe

The canonical scene's installer (section 5), plus the ScriptableObject form:

```csharp
using Onity.Composition;        // BindReactiveProperty
using Onity.DI;                 // OnityContainer
using Onity.Unity.Installers;   // MonoInstaller, BindPooledFactory, BindScriptableObject
using Onity.Unity.Messaging;    // BindMessageChannel
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class GameInstaller : MonoInstaller
{
    [SerializeField] private GameConfig m_config;            // a ScriptableObject that implements IGameConfig
    [SerializeField] private HitMarker m_hitMarkerPrefab;
    [SerializeField] private Transform m_hitMarkerRoot;

    public override void InstallBindings(OnityContainer container)
    {
        // Member-inject the asset, then bind it as the read-only contract (caller-owned).
        container.BindScriptableObject<IGameConfig, GameConfig>(m_config);

        // ReactiveProperty<int> and IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<int>; the scope disposes it.
        container.BindReactiveProperty(initialValue: 100);

        // IPublisher<PlayerDamaged> and ISubscriber<PlayerDamaged> on the scope's message broker,
        // the same channel OnityEvent and OnityEventHub use.
        container.BindMessageChannel<PlayerDamaged>();

        // IFactory<HitMarker> to spawn and IPool<HitMarker> to release; the scope disposes the pool.
        container.BindPooledFactory(m_hitMarkerPrefab, m_hitMarkerRoot, defaultCapacity: 8, maxSize: 32);

        // The container constructs it, runs Initialize() at Build() and disposes it with the scope.
        container.BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<HealthService>().AsSingle();
    }
}
```

`MessageBroker` (with `IMessageBroker`) and `OnityEventHub` are bound by every context, so a service
injects either with no installer line. `BindMessageChannel<T>()` is only needed to inject `IPublisher<T>`
or `ISubscriber<T>` directly, and it resolves `IMessageBroker` at bind time; in a bare container without
a context, bind `MessageBroker` first or use `DeclareMessage<T>()` (section 4.4, Recipe E).

## 3. Reactive: Onity.Reactive and the Onity.Unity.Reactive bridges

Push-based and hot by default. The one contract is `IOnityObservable<T>`: `Subject<T>`,
`ReactiveProperty<T>`, every operator and `Observe<T>()` return it. `Observer<T>` is
`public delegate void Observer<T>(T value)`; the `Subscribe(Action<T>)` you normally write is an
extension that stores the action in the subscription node, which the source invokes directly. A plain
subscription allocates one object (the node, which is also the `IDisposable` you receive); steady-state
`OnNext` and `SetValue` allocate nothing. `OnityObserver<T>` is the abstract observer-object form with
`OnNextCore`, `OnErrorCore`, `OnCompletedCore` and `OnDisposed`; gameplay code rarely needs it.

### 3.1 Primitives

```csharp
using System;
using Onity.Reactive;           // Subject<T>, ReactiveProperty<T>, CompositeDisposable, AddTo
using UnityEngine;

// Subject<T>: a multicast source. OnNext allocates nothing in steady state.
Subject<int> damage = new Subject<int>();
IDisposable token = damage.Subscribe(amount => Debug.Log(amount));
damage.OnNext(10);
token.Dispose();
damage.Dispose();                                    // OnNext and Subscribe throw ObjectDisposedException afterwards

// ReactiveProperty<T>: a value plus change notification. Equal values are skipped (built-in DistinctUntilChanged).
ReactiveProperty<int> health = new ReactiveProperty<int>(100);
health.Value = 90;                                   // notifies only when the value changed
bool changed = health.SetValue(90);                  // false: same value, nothing published
IDisposable current = health.Subscribe(value => Debug.Log(value));                          // logs 90 now, then each change
IDisposable changes = health.Subscribe(value => Debug.Log(value), emitCurrentValue: false);  // changes only
IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<int> readOnly = health;    // hand this to consumers: Value plus Subscribe, no operators
current.Dispose();                                   // every Subscribe result is kept and disposed by its owner
changes.Dispose();

// CompositeDisposable: a lifetime bag for plain C# owners.
CompositeDisposable bag = new CompositeDisposable();
health.Subscribe(value => { }).AddTo(bag);
bag.Clear();                                         // dispose everything, keep the bag
bag.Dispose();                                       // final; a later Add disposes the item at once

// A custom source: the function receives the observer and returns the disposable that ends the subscription.
IOnityObservable<int> healthStream = new OnityObservable<int>(observer => readOnly.Subscribe(observer));
```

`IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<T>` declares only `Value` and `Subscribe(observer, emitCurrentValue = true)`;
it does not implement `IOnityObservable<T>`, so the operators do not apply to it. Inject the
`ReactiveProperty<T>` itself where `Where` or another operator is needed, or wrap it once as above.
`ReactiveProperty<T>.Dispose()` does not notify observers.

### 3.2 Synchronous operators (OnityObservableExtensions)

Each returns `IOnityObservable<T>`, allocates one sink node when it is subscribed and forwards each value
without allocating (`Where` followed by `Select` is fused into one sink):

`Where(Predicate<T>)`, `Select(Func<TSource, TResult>)`, `DistinctUntilChanged(IEqualityComparer<T> = null)`,
`Skip(int)`, `SkipWhile(Predicate<T>)`, `Take(int)`, `TakeWhile(Predicate<T>)`, `StartWith(T)`,
`Scan<TState>(seed, Func<TState, T, TState>)`, `Pairwise() -> IOnityObservable<OnityPair<T>>`
(`Previous`, `Current`), `Buffer(int count) -> IOnityObservable<IReadOnlyList<T>>`,
`Merge(params IOnityObservable<T>[])`, `CombineLatest<T1, T2, TResult>(other, selector)` (two sources),
`Sample<TSignal>(sampler)`, `TakeUntilCancellation(CancellationToken)`, `Subscribe(Action<T>)`,
`Subscribe(Action<T>, Action<Exception>, Action<OnityResult>)`, `FirstAsync(CancellationToken) -> Task<T>`,
`ToTask(this IOnityObservable<Unit>, CancellationToken) -> Task`.

Factories on the static `OnityObservable`: `FromEvent<T>(addHandler, removeHandler)`, `Return<T>(value)`,
`Empty<T>()`. There is no `Never`, `Create` or `Defer`, and no `Window`, `Zip`, `Switch`, `Concat`,
`Publish`, `Share` or `RefCount` on `IOnityObservable<T>`.

```csharp
// Fragment, in a service that holds ReactiveProperty<int> m_health and an injected IOnityScopeLifetime scope:
m_health.Where(value => value <= 0)
        .Subscribe(_ => m_events.Publish(new PlayerDied()))
        .AddTo(scope);
```

The core operators carry no error channel: `onError` is raised only by sources that report faults
(`OnityTask.ToObservable()`, `IOnityAsyncEnumerable<T>.AsObservable()`), and `onCompleted` runs when the
subscription is disposed. `TakeUntil(ct)` and `TakeUntilCancellation(ct)` stop the stream silently.

### 3.3 Time and async operators (OnityObservableAsyncExtensions and the thread-pool operators)

Each time operator takes an optional `OnityTimeProvider`. Without one it waits on
`OnityTimeProvider.System` (wall-clock `Task.Delay`); in gameplay pass one of `OnityTimeProviders`
(`Onity.Unity.Reactive`: `UpdateScaled`, `UpdateUnscaled`, `UpdateRealtime` and the `Fixed*` and `Late*`
forms) so the wait follows a Unity loop and time mode. In EditMode tests subclass `OnityTimeProvider`
and override `DelayAsync`; no manual or fake provider ships.

- `Debounce(TimeSpan dueTime, OnityTimeProvider = null)`: emit the last value after a quiet window.
- `Throttle(TimeSpan interval, OnityTimeProvider = null)`: emit the first value, then drop values until
  the interval elapses (leading edge). `ThrottleLast(TimeSpan interval, OnityTimeProvider = null)`: emit
  the latest value once per interval (trailing edge). UniRx's `Throttle` corresponds to `Debounce`.
- `Buffer(TimeSpan timeSpan, OnityTimeProvider = null)`: the values gathered in each window.
- `TakeUntil(CancellationToken)` and `TakeUntil(Task)`: stop on a signal; `TakeUntilCancellation(token)`
  is the synchronous form.
- `SelectAwait(Func<T, CancellationToken, ValueTask<TResult>>)` and
  `WhereAwait(Func<T, CancellationToken, ValueTask<bool>>)`: sequential async projection and filter,
  one value at a time, run inside `Task.Run`; values arrive on the thread that completed the delegate. A
  delegate that throws ends that subscription without notifying the subscriber.
- `ObserveOnThreadPool()`: re-post values onto one worker in source order.
  `SelectOnThreadPool(selector, maxConcurrency = 0)` (also with a token-taking selector): a CPU-bound
  projection on up to `maxConcurrency` workers (`0` is the processor count); results emit as workers
  finish, so pass `1` when order matters. An exception on the worker goes to
  `OnityObservableExceptionHandler`.
- `ObserveOn(OnityFrameProvider)` queues values onto a frame provider's next tick;
  `ObserveOnMainThread()` (`Onity.Unity.Reactive`) is `ObserveOn(OnityFrameProviders.Update)`, and the
  required hop before a subscriber touches `UnityEngine` after `SelectAwait`, `WhereAwait` or a
  thread-pool operator. `Delay(float seconds, bool useUnscaledTime = false)` delays each value with a
  Unity timer.

### 3.4 Unity bridges: frame loops, timers, lifetime

```csharp
using System.Threading;
using Onity.DI;                 // [Inject], IOnityScopeLifetime, AddTo(IOnityScopeLifetime)
using Onity.Reactive;           // Subscribe, CompositeDisposable, AddTo(CompositeDisposable)
using Onity.Unity.Reactive;     // OnityUnityObservable, AddTo(Component), TakeUntilDestroy, TakeUntilDisable
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class FrameLoops : MonoBehaviour
{
    [Inject] private IOnityScopeLifetime m_scope;                 // the scope of the context above this component

    private readonly CompositeDisposable m_bag = new CompositeDisposable();
    private readonly CancellationTokenSource m_stop = new CancellationTokenSource();

    private void Start()
    {
        // Frame loops are IOnityObservable<Unit> (Unit lives in Onity.Core): one value per frame from a shared
        // pump component. The lifetime helpers extend the IDisposable that Subscribe returns, so they go AFTER it.
        OnityUnityObservable.EveryUpdate().Subscribe(_ => Tick()).AddTo(this);                  // disposed when this Component is destroyed (same as TakeUntilDestroy)
        OnityUnityObservable.EveryFixedUpdate().Subscribe(_ => Tick()).TakeUntilDisable(this);  // disposed when this Behaviour is disabled, and on destroy
        OnityUnityObservable.EveryLateUpdate().Subscribe(_ => Tick()).TakeUntilDestroy(this);
        OnityUnityObservable.EveryUpdate(m_stop.Token).Subscribe(_ => Tick()).AddTo(m_bag);     // stops when the token is canceled; Onity.Reactive bag

        // Timers: one Unit after two seconds (useUnscaledTime overload); the tick count, starting at 1, every second.
        OnityUnityObservable.Timer(2f).Subscribe(_ => Debug.Log("two seconds")).AddTo(m_scope);  // Onity.DI: disposed with the scope
        OnityUnityObservable.Interval(1f).Subscribe(tick => Debug.Log(tick)).AddTo(this);        // IOnityObservable<int>
    }

    private void OnDestroy()
    {
        m_stop.Cancel();
        m_stop.Dispose();
        m_bag.Dispose();
    }

    private void Tick()
    {
    }
}
```

The Unity helpers take a `Component` or `Behaviour`; pass `this` from a `MonoBehaviour`. There is no
`AddTo(GameObject)` overload. On first use they add an `OnityLifetimeNotifier` component to the owner,
which disposes the registered subscriptions from its `OnDisable` and `OnDestroy`. The
`EveryUpdate(OnityUnityThreadMode ...)` overloads add a job boundary around each frame signal
(`SingleThread`, `JobMultiThread`, `BurstJobMultiThread`, `DotsEventDriven`); observers still run on the
main thread. For a service that ticks for the life of its scope, implement `IOnityTickable` instead of
subscribing to `EveryUpdate()`.

### 3.5 Gameplay recipes

```csharp
// Recipe A: a threshold on current state. ReactiveProperty replays its value, so this fires at once when already dead.
// Fragment of HealthService's constructor (ReactiveProperty<int> health, OnityEventHub events, IOnityScopeLifetime scope):
health.Where(value => value <= 0)
      .Subscribe(_ => events.Publish(new PlayerDied()))
      .AddTo(scope);                             // unsubscribed when the scope ends
```

```csharp
// Recipe B: tick every frame until this Behaviour is disabled. Fragment of HitMarker.OnEnable:
OnityUnityObservable.EveryUpdate()
    .Subscribe(_ => Fade())                       // one step of the fade per frame
    .TakeUntilDisable(this);                      // disposed on disable, and on destroy
```

```csharp
// Recipe C: debounce in scaled game time. Fragment of HealthHud.OnEnable:
OnityEvent.Observe<PlayerDamaged>(this)
          .Debounce(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), OnityTimeProviders.UpdateScaled)
          .Subscribe(_ => HideHitMarkers())
          .TakeUntilDisable(this);
```

```csharp
// Recipe D: await the first matching value (reactive -> Task). Fragment of a service that holds OnityEventHub m_events:
public Task WaitForDeathAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    return m_events.Observe<PlayerDied>().FirstAsync(ct);   // completes on the first PlayerDied, then unsubscribes
}
// For OnityTask code: m_events.Observe<PlayerDied>().FirstOnityTask(ct)  (Onity.Unity.Async)
```

```csharp
// Recipe E: Input System reactive bridge (requires ENABLE_INPUT_SYSTEM).
using Onity.Reactive;           // Subscribe
using Onity.Unity.Input;        // PerformedAsObservable, StartedAsObservable, CanceledAsObservable
using Onity.Unity.Reactive;     // TakeUntilDisable
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

public sealed class FireControl : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private InputActionReference m_fire;

    private void OnEnable()
    {
        m_fire.action.PerformedAsObservable()
              .Subscribe(_ => Fire())
              .TakeUntilDisable(this);
    }

    private void Fire()
    {
    }
}
```

`OnityReactiveInputPlayer` (`Onity.Unity.Input`) routes an `InputActionAsset` into button, `Vector2`,
`float` and long-press streams (`GetButtonObservable`, `GetVector2Observable`, `GetFloatObservable`,
`GetLongPressObservable`, `GetLongPressProgressObservable`) with a context stack; the long-press streams
exist only on this type.

## 4. Events: Onity.Messaging and the Onity.Unity.Messaging bridges

Typed pub/sub over the scope's broker. `MessageChannel<T>` delivers one message type: `Publish`
allocates nothing in steady state, a handler may unsubscribe from inside a publish pass, and the channel
throws after `Dispose()`. Publish and subscribe on the Unity main thread; the broker locks its channel
table, never the publish path. Handlers run in subscription order until an unsubscribe outside a publish pass moves the
last handler into the freed slot, so the order is not a priority contract.

### 4.1 Surface

```csharp
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using Onity.Messaging;          // IMessageBroker, IPublisher<T>, ISubscriber<T>, MessageChannelDiagnostics
using UnityEngine;

// IMessageBroker: the source of typed channels, one per message type, created on first request.
IPublisher<PlayerDamaged> publisher = broker.GetPublisher<PlayerDamaged>();
ISubscriber<PlayerDamaged> subscriber = broker.GetSubscriber<PlayerDamaged>();

publisher.Publish(new PlayerDamaged(10));
IDisposable token = subscriber.Subscribe(message => Debug.Log(message.Amount));

// Broker-level convenience (MessageBrokerExtensions):
broker.Publish(new PlayerDamaged(10));
IDisposable token2 = broker.Subscribe<PlayerDamaged>(message => Debug.Log(message.Amount));

// Diagnostics into a caller-supplied list (MessageBroker only):
List<MessageChannelDiagnostics> diagnostics = new List<MessageChannelDiagnostics>(8);
broker.GetDiagnostics(diagnostics);          // each entry: MessageType and SubscriberCount
int channels = broker.ChannelCount;
```

`MessageHandler<TMessage>` is `public delegate void MessageHandler<TMessage>(TMessage message)`. Keyed
routing ships as `KeyedMessageChannel<TKey, TMessage>` (`IKeyedPublisher`, `IKeyedSubscriber`; its
members take a `key` first: `channel.Subscribe(1, handler)`, `channel.Publish(1, message)`), and awaited
delivery as `AsyncMessageChannel<TMessage>` (`IAsyncPublisher.PublishAsync(message, ct)`,
`IAsyncSubscriber.Subscribe(handler)`, sequential), with `PublishOnityTask` and `SubscribeOnityTask`
(`Onity.Unity.Async`) as the `OnityTask` forms. The broker does not create keyed or async channels;
construct them, or use `DeclareAsyncMessage<T>()`. Not shipped: buffered or replayed messages, handler
priority, request-response. Model "the current value for a late subscriber" as a `ReactiveProperty<T>`.

A handler that throws propagates out of `Publish` (or faults `PublishAsync`), and the remaining handlers
for that message do not run; this also holds for observers of a stream from `Observe<T>()`, which run
inside the channel's handler. Catch inside the handler when one listener must not break the others.

### 4.2 Reactive bridge: Observe

`broker.Observe<T>()`, `subscriber.Observe<T>()` (`OnityMessageReactiveExtensions`,
`Onity.Unity.Messaging`), `OnityEventHub.Observe<T>()` and `OnityEvent.Observe<T>()` return
`IOnityObservable<T>`, so a message flows into the operator chain without an adapter. The hub caches one
stream per message type.

```csharp
using Onity.Reactive;           // Where, Select, Subscribe
using Onity.Unity.Messaging;    // Observe<T> on IMessageBroker and ISubscriber<T>
using Onity.Unity.Reactive;     // AddTo
using UnityEngine;              // Debug

broker.Observe<PlayerDamaged>()
      .Where(message => message.Amount > 0)
      .Select(message => message.Amount)
      .Subscribe(amount => Debug.Log($"Took {amount}"))
      .AddTo(this);
```

### 4.3 OnityEvent and OnityEventHub

`OnityEvent` (`Onity.Unity`) is the static shorthand for `MonoBehaviour` code. The no-owner members use
the default context: the most recently activated `SceneContext`, then `ProjectContext.Instance`, then
any other active context. The owner members use the context on the owner component or its nearest
parent, with the default context as fallback; use them inside a `GameObjectContext`. Without any active
context they throw `InvalidOperationException`.

```csharp
using System;
using Onity.Reactive;           // IOnityObservable<T>
using Onity.Unity;              // OnityEvent
using Onity.Unity.Messaging;    // OnityEventHub

OnityEvent.Publish(new PlayerDamaged(10));                                   // default context
OnityEvent.Publish(this, new PlayerDamaged(10));                             // nearest context above this component
IDisposable token = OnityEvent.Subscribe<PlayerDamaged>(this, OnDamaged);    // also disposed when this component is destroyed
IOnityObservable<PlayerDamaged> stream = OnityEvent.Observe<PlayerDamaged>(this);
OnityEventHub hub = OnityEvent.GetEventHub(this);                            // TryGetEventHub returns false instead of throwing
```

`OnityEventHub` (`Onity.Unity.Messaging`) is the scoped facade a service injects: `Publish<TMessage>(message)`,
`Subscribe<TMessage>(handler) -> IDisposable` and `Observe<TMessage>() -> IOnityObservable<TMessage>`. It
wraps the scope's broker, implements no interfaces, and every context binds it as itself. `IMessageBroker`
offers the same calls when one service handles several message types.

### 4.4 Event recipes

```csharp
// Recipe A: publish a typed message from Unity code through the nearest context (the canonical DamageZone).
using Onity.Unity;              // OnityEvent
using UnityEngine;

public readonly struct PlayerDamaged
{
    public readonly int Amount;

    public PlayerDamaged(int amount)
    {
        Amount = amount;
    }
}

public sealed class DamageZone : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private int m_damage = 25;

    private void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
    {
        OnityEvent.Publish(this, new PlayerDamaged(m_damage));   // the nearest context's channel
    }
}
```

```csharp
// Recipe B: subscribe in OnEnable, dispose in OnDisable, so a re-enabled component does not subscribe twice.
using System;
using Onity.Unity;              // OnityEvent
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class DamageFlash : MonoBehaviour
{
    private IDisposable m_subscription;

    private void OnEnable()
    {
        m_subscription = OnityEvent.Subscribe<PlayerDamaged>(this, OnDamaged);   // also disposed on destroy
    }

    private void OnDisable()
    {
        m_subscription?.Dispose();
        m_subscription = null;
    }

    private void OnDamaged(PlayerDamaged message)
    {
        // Flash the screen.
    }
}
```

```csharp
// Recipe C: direction-only injection (needs BindMessageChannel<PlayerDamaged>() in the installer).
// The canonical HealthService takes the subscriber side and ties the subscription to its scope.
using System;
using Onity.DI;                 // IOnityScopeLifetime, AddTo(scope)
using Onity.Messaging;          // ISubscriber<T>
using Onity.Reactive;           // ReactiveProperty<T>

public sealed class HealthService
{
    private readonly ReactiveProperty<int> m_health;

    public HealthService(ReactiveProperty<int> health, ISubscriber<PlayerDamaged> damage, IOnityScopeLifetime scope)
    {
        m_health = health;
        damage.Subscribe(OnDamaged).AddTo(scope);     // unsubscribed when the scope ends
    }

    private void OnDamaged(PlayerDamaged message)
    {
        m_health.SetValue(Math.Max(0, m_health.Value - message.Amount));
    }
}
```

```csharp
// Recipe D: broker-direct, engine-free (tests and plain services).
using System;
using Onity.Messaging;          // MessageBroker, Publish, Subscribe

using MessageBroker broker = new MessageBroker();
IDisposable token = broker.Subscribe<PlayerDamaged>(message => { /* handle */ });
broker.Publish(new PlayerDamaged(10));
token.Dispose();
```

Recipe E, two ways to bind `IPublisher<T>` and `ISubscriber<T>`: `container.BindMessageChannel<T>()`
(`Onity.Unity.Messaging`) binds the scope broker's own channel, so `OnityEvent`, `OnityEventHub` and the
injected interfaces share one channel; it resolves `IMessageBroker` at bind time, which a context binds
before installers run. `container.DeclareMessage<T>()` (`Onity.Composition`) creates a standalone
`MessageChannel<T>` the broker never sees and binds it as `MessageChannel<T>`, `IPublisher<T>` and
`ISubscriber<T>`; the scope disposes it. Use `DeclareMessage` for a channel private to the services that
inject it, or as the stand-in for the broker in a scene-free test (section 5), never for a channel that
`OnityEvent` must reach.

## 5. End-to-end: the canonical scene

One scene scope owns the player's health. `DamageZone` publishes `PlayerDamaged`; `HealthService`
(constructor-injected) lowers the health and regenerates it on an async loop that ends with the scope;
`HealthHud` shows the health and spawns a pooled `HitMarker` that it releases after a delay; one
installer binds all of it. [Getting Started](../Getting-Started.md) builds the same files step by step.

```csharp
// PlayerDamaged.cs: the message. Plain C#, nothing from Onity.
public readonly struct PlayerDamaged
{
    public readonly int Amount;

    public PlayerDamaged(int amount)
    {
        Amount = amount;
    }
}
```

```csharp
// GameInstaller.cs: the scene's bindings.
using Onity.Composition;        // BindReactiveProperty
using Onity.DI;                 // OnityContainer
using Onity.Unity.Installers;   // MonoInstaller, BindPooledFactory
using Onity.Unity.Messaging;    // BindMessageChannel
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class GameInstaller : MonoInstaller
{
    [SerializeField] private HitMarker m_hitMarkerPrefab;
    [SerializeField] private Transform m_hitMarkerRoot;

    public override void InstallBindings(OnityContainer container)
    {
        // ReactiveProperty<int> and IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<int>; the scope disposes it.
        container.BindReactiveProperty(initialValue: 100);

        // IPublisher<PlayerDamaged> and ISubscriber<PlayerDamaged> on the scope's message broker,
        // the same channel OnityEvent and OnityEventHub use.
        container.BindMessageChannel<PlayerDamaged>();

        // IFactory<HitMarker> to spawn and IPool<HitMarker> to release; the scope disposes the pool.
        container.BindPooledFactory(m_hitMarkerPrefab, m_hitMarkerRoot, defaultCapacity: 8, maxSize: 32);

        // The container constructs it, runs Initialize() at Build() and disposes it with the scope.
        container.BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<HealthService>().AsSingle();
    }
}
```

```csharp
// HealthService.cs: a plain C# service. The container builds it; the scope owns its subscription and its loop.
using System;
using System.Threading;
using Onity.DI;                 // IOnityInitializable, IOnityScopeLifetime, AddTo(scope)
using Onity.Messaging;          // ISubscriber<T>
using Onity.Reactive;           // ReactiveProperty<T>
using Onity.Unity.Async;        // OnityTask, OnityTaskVoid

public sealed class HealthService : IOnityInitializable
{
    private const int k_maxHealth = 100;
    private const float k_regenerationInterval = 1f;

    private readonly ReactiveProperty<int> m_health;
    private readonly IOnityScopeLifetime m_scope;

    public HealthService(ReactiveProperty<int> health, ISubscriber<PlayerDamaged> damage, IOnityScopeLifetime scope)
    {
        m_health = health;
        m_scope = scope;
        damage.Subscribe(OnDamaged).AddTo(scope);     // unsubscribed when the scope ends
    }

    public void Initialize()
    {
        RegenerateAsync(m_scope.Token).Forget();      // the token is canceled before the scope disposes its services
    }

    private void OnDamaged(PlayerDamaged message)
    {
        m_health.SetValue(Math.Max(0, m_health.Value - message.Amount));
    }

    private async OnityTaskVoid RegenerateAsync(CancellationToken token)
    {
        while (!token.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            await OnityTask.Delay(k_regenerationInterval, token);
            m_health.SetValue(Math.Min(k_maxHealth, m_health.Value + 1));
        }
    }
}
```

```csharp
// HealthHud.cs: a thin MonoBehaviour. Unity constructs it, so the context injects members.
using System.Threading;
using Onity.DI;                 // Inject
using Onity.Factory;            // IFactory<T>
using Onity.Pooling;            // IPool<T>
using Onity.Reactive;           // IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<T>, Where
using Onity.Unity;              // OnityEvent
using Onity.Unity.Async;        // OnityTask, OnityTaskVoid, GetScopeCancellationToken
using Onity.Unity.Reactive;     // TakeUntilDisable
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class HealthHud : MonoBehaviour
{
    private const float k_hitMarkerSeconds = 0.5f;

    // Unity constructs MonoBehaviours, so the context injects members instead of a constructor.
    [Inject] private IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<int> m_health;
    [Inject] private IFactory<HitMarker> m_hitMarkers;
    [Inject] private IPool<HitMarker> m_hitMarkerPool;

    private void OnEnable()
    {
        m_health.Subscribe(value => Debug.Log($"Health: {value}"))   // emits the current value first
                .TakeUntilDisable(this);

        OnityEvent.Observe<PlayerDamaged>(this)                       // the channel HealthService subscribes to
                  .Where(message => message.Amount >= 10)
                  .Subscribe(ShowHit)
                  .TakeUntilDisable(this);
    }

    private void ShowHit(PlayerDamaged message)
    {
        HitMarker marker = m_hitMarkers.Create();                     // taken from the pool
        marker.Show(message.Amount);
        ReleaseLaterAsync(marker, this.GetScopeCancellationToken()).Forget();
    }

    private async OnityTaskVoid ReleaseLaterAsync(HitMarker marker, CancellationToken token)
    {
        await OnityTask.Delay(k_hitMarkerSeconds, token);             // ends with the scope
        m_hitMarkerPool.Release(marker);                              // back to the pool, exactly once
    }
}
```

```csharp
// HitMarker.cs: the pooled prefab. PrefabComponentPool<T> activates it, then calls OnPoolGet; OnPoolRelease, then deactivates.
using Onity.Pooling;            // IPoolHooks
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class HitMarker : MonoBehaviour, IPoolHooks
{
    public void Show(int amount)
    {
        // Position the marker and display the amount.
    }

    public void OnPoolGet()
    {
        // Reset per-use state when the pool hands this instance out.
    }

    public void OnPoolRelease()
    {
        // Clear references when the instance returns to the pool.
    }
}
```

```csharp
// DamageZone.cs: the publisher.
using Onity.Unity;              // OnityEvent
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class DamageZone : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private int m_damage = 25;

    private void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
    {
        OnityEvent.Publish(this, new PlayerDamaged(m_damage));   // the nearest context's channel
    }
}
```

Scene wiring: create an empty GameObject `SceneContext`, add the `SceneContext` component (search for
it in Add Component; there is no Onity submenu) and the `GameInstaller` component, drag `GameInstaller`
into the context's Installers list, assign the `HitMarker` prefab and a root transform, and place
`HealthHud` and `DamageZone` under the `SceneContext` object so the context injects them in `Awake`. The
context builds the container in `Awake` (which runs `HealthService.Initialize`), injects the hierarchy,
runs the async build in `Start`, pumps the lifecycle ticks, and disposes the container in `OnDestroy`,
which cancels the scope token first.

The service runs without a scene. `DeclareMessage<T>` stands in for the broker channel a context would
bind, and binding the container as `IOnityScopeLifetime` gives the service the same scope it gets from
a context:

```csharp
// HealthServiceTests.cs: an EditMode test.
using NUnit.Framework;
using Onity.Composition;        // BindReactiveProperty, DeclareMessage
using Onity.DI;
using Onity.Messaging;
using Onity.Reactive;

public sealed class HealthServiceTests
{
    [Test]
    public void Damage_lowers_health()
    {
        using OnityContainer container = new OnityContainer();
        ReactiveProperty<int> health = container.BindReactiveProperty(initialValue: 100);
        MessageChannel<PlayerDamaged> damage = container.DeclareMessage<PlayerDamaged>();  // standalone channel; a context would bind the broker's
        container.BindInstance<IOnityScopeLifetime>(container);                              // what a context binds for you
        container.BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<HealthService>().AsSingle();
        container.Build();                                                                    // constructs HealthService and runs Initialize()

        damage.Publish(new PlayerDamaged(30));

        Assert.AreEqual(70, health.Value);
    }   // Dispose cancels the scope token, which ends the regeneration loop
}
```

### 5.1 Context scoping: project versus scene

Put project-scope services on the `ProjectContext` prefab, not on a `SceneContext`. Anything that must
live for the whole session and survive scene loads (catalogs, saves, currency, inventory, settings,
audio, scene flow) belongs in an installer on the auto-loaded `ProjectContext`. Per-scene collaborators
(a match's rules, presentation and spawn factories, per-screen controllers) belong on that scene's
`SceneContext`. A `SceneContext` is created on every scene load, so a session-wide singleton bound
there is rebuilt per scene and does not persist. A scene installer depends on project services without
rebinding them; the parent chain resolves them.

| Context | Lifetime | Execution order | Parent it resolves | Use for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ProjectContext` | one persistent instance (`ProjectContext.Instance`, `DontDestroyOnLoad`) | `-10000` | none | session-wide services |
| `SceneContext` | rebuilt per scene load | `-9800` | its Project Context field, else `ProjectContext.Instance` | per-scene services |
| `GameObjectContext` | lives with its GameObject subtree | `-9700` | the nearest `OnityContext` above it (Find Parent In Hierarchy), else `ProjectContext.Instance` (Fallback To Project Context) | a sub-scope for one prefab or subtree |

Every context binds the container, `IResolver`, `IOnityScopeLifetime`, itself, `MessageBroker` with
its interfaces and `OnityEventHub`, runs the `MonoInstaller` components in its Installers list, builds,
and member-injects the MonoBehaviours under its own GameObject (Auto Inject Hierarchy, on by default).
`Run Async Build Callbacks` (on by default) runs `BuildAsync` in `Start`. `ProjectContext` is loaded
before the first scene by `ProjectContextBootstrap` from `Resources/Onity/ProjectContext` when none
exists; create the prefab once with `Onity/Contexts/Create ProjectContext Prefab` (it is saved at
`Assets/Resources/Onity/ProjectContext.prefab`), then add the project installers to its Installers
list. A missing prefab is silent and leaves `ProjectContext.Instance` null.

```text
ProjectContext (Assets/Resources/Onity/ProjectContext.prefab)
    Installers: [ProjectInstaller]                 // persists across scenes
SceneContext
    Installers: [GameInstaller]                    // per scene; resolves the project services above
```

---

## 6. DO and DON'T

DO:

- DO put domain logic in plain C# services with constructor injection; keep MonoBehaviours thin, with
  `[Inject]` members.
- DO finish every binding with `AsSingle()`, `AsScoped()` or `AsTransient()` (or
  `FromSubContainerResolve`); `Bind<T>()` and `To<C>()` alone register nothing.
- DO retain every `Subscribe` result: `TakeUntilDisable(this)` for subscriptions made in `OnEnable`,
  `AddTo(this)` for ones that live until destroy, `AddTo(scope)` in a scope service,
  `AddTo(compositeDisposable)` elsewhere.
- DO use `BindInterfacesAndSelfTo<C>().AsSingle()` to share one instance across a concrete type and its
  interfaces.
- DO model current state as a `ReactiveProperty<T>` (bound with `BindReactiveProperty`) and past-tense
  notifications as messages (section 9).
- DO give every async loop a token from its owner: `IOnityScopeLifetime.Token` in a service,
  `GetScopeCancellationToken()` or `GetCancellationTokenOnDestroy()` in a component. Use
  `async OnityTaskVoid` or `Forget(handler)` for fire-and-forget work.
- DO pass an `OnityTimeProvider` (for example `OnityTimeProviders.UpdateScaled`) to `Debounce`,
  `Throttle`, `ThrottleLast` and `Buffer` in gameplay.
- DO assign `OnityObservableExceptionHandler.Handler` at startup (for example `Debug.LogException`);
  without it a subscriber exception inside `Subject<T>.OnNext` is swallowed.
- DO spawn reusable objects through a pool (`BindPooledFactory`: `IFactory<T>` to spawn, `IPool<T>` to
  release; `OnityObjectPool<T>` for plain C#) instead of `Instantiate` and `Destroy` in gameplay loops.
- DO use `AsScoped()` for one instance per resolving scope, and `WithId` or `WhenInjectedInto` for a
  second implementation of one contract.
- DO change scenes through one `IOnitySceneService` bound on the `ProjectContext` with
  `container.BindSceneService(...)`, and check the awaited `OnitySceneResult`: `Busy`, `InvalidTarget` and
  `ReadinessTimedOut` are results, not exceptions. The destination reads its enter data with
  `OnitySceneTransitionStore.TryGetEnterData<T>(gameObject.scene, out T)` while it installs.

DON'T:

- DON'T add bindings after `Build()`; installers run before it. Only `Unbind` and `Rebind` change a built
  scope, and build callbacks throw after the build.
- DON'T `Resolve<T>()` inside `Update`, `FixedUpdate` or `LateUpdate`; inject once and keep the reference.
- DON'T `new` a service that has dependencies; bind it and let the container construct it (`ONITY006`).
- DON'T expect two separate `Bind<I>().To<C>()` calls to share one instance.
- DON'T hand-build registries when collection injection fits; bind each implementation and request a
  collection shape.
- DON'T resolve an open generic definition; bind the open definition and resolve a closed form.
- DON'T add a second `[Inject]` constructor, a setterless `[Inject]` property, an `[Inject]` indexer or a
  generic `[Inject]` method; each throws `OnityBindingException`.
- DON'T apply operators to an `IReadOnlyReactiveProperty<T>`; it is not an `IOnityObservable<T>`. Inject
  the `ReactiveProperty<T>` or wrap it.
- DON'T expect `OnityEvent` or `OnityEventHub` to reach a `DeclareMessage<T>` channel; use
  `BindMessageChannel<T>` for a shared channel.
- DON'T touch `UnityEngine` members after `SelectAwait`, `WhereAwait` or a thread-pool operator without
  `ObserveOnMainThread()` first; DON'T publish to a broker or `Subject<T>` from a background thread.
- DON'T let a message handler throw unless every later handler for that message may be skipped; the
  exception propagates out of `Publish`.
- DON'T release a pooled item twice, use it after `Release`, or `Destroy` it; release it exactly once
  (10.5). DON'T assume the container disposes a pool you built; `BindPooledFactory(prefab, ...)` pools are
  scope-owned, pools you pass in are yours until `pool.AddTo(container)` (10.4).
- DON'T bind the scene service, `OnityCoveredSceneTransition` or `OnityScenePreloader` on a
  `SceneContext`: the scene that asks is the one a Single load unloads. DON'T unload by scene name when two
  instances can exist; pass the `Scene` an `OnitySceneResult` returned. DON'T start the next scene load
  from a `State` callback; start it from `Completed` or after the awaited result.
- DON'T write `async void`; DON'T await a pooled `OnityTask` twice without `Preserve()`.
- DON'T use `System.Linq` in package code; write plain loops and avoid allocations in hot paths.
- DON'T call an API that is not in this guide or the source on the assumption of Zenject, VContainer,
  R3, UniRx, MessagePipe or UniTask parity: no `Instantiate(args)`, no fluent factory bodies, no
  `Window`, `Zip`, `Switch`, `Concat`, `Publish`, `Share` or `RefCount` on `IOnityObservable<T>` (the
  async streams have `Zip`, `Concat`, `Publish` and `Queue`), no buffered or replay messages, no handler
  priority, no request-response.
